def: The most common form of Francisella tularensis infection, with a skin ulcer at the inoculation site and tender enlarged regional lymph nodes, usually after tick bite or handling rabbits.
A family of small non-enveloped, single-stranded RNA viruses that includes norovirus, the leading cause of epidemic viral gastroenteritis on cruise ships.
Located below the occipital bone at the back of the skull. Suboccipital lymphadenopathy, with posterior auricular nodes, is a classic finding in rubella.
Relating to both the respiratory and upper digestive tracts, e.g., aerodigestive foreign bodies in the airway or esophagus.
Joints between the radius and ulna, proximal and distal, allowing forearm pronation and supination.
Describing red cells with normal hemoglobin content (normal MCHC), so they look normal in color on a smear. Normocytic normochromic anemia occurs in anemia of chronic disease and acute blood loss.
Pale, clay-colored stool lacking bile pigment, signaling biliary obstruction; in an infant with prolonged jaundice, suspect biliary atresia.
Located behind the ear, such as postauricular lymph nodes or the postauricular skin affected by seborrheic dermatitis.
Blue-gray flat birthmark (Mongolian spot) from melanocytes trapped in the dermis, usually over the sacrum in dark-skinned infants. It is benign and fades.
A fluorescent dye that binds the band 3 protein on red cell membranes; reduced binding on flow cytometry (EMA test) diagnoses hereditary spherocytosis.
Inability to concentrate urine, producing persistently dilute urine. Seen in sickle cell disease and trait, from medullary damage.
Abnormally low reticulocyte count, indicating decreased red cell production. Parvovirus B19 causes transient reticulocytopenia in hemolytic anemias.
The P blood group antigen, a glycosphingolipid that is the cellular receptor for parvovirus B19 on erythroid progenitors.
Obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct in infants, causing tearing and eye discharge; usually resolves with massage by age one.
A carcinogenic aromatic amine used in dyes, linked to urothelial (bladder) cancer.
The space of Retzius behind the pubic bones and in front of the bladder. Urine leaks into it in posterior urethral injury.
Located above the sella turcica. Suprasellar masses such as craniopharyngioma and pituitary adenomas can compress the optic chiasm.
Relating to the dense petrous part of the temporal bone, which houses the inner ear; fractures cause hearing loss, facial nerve palsy and hemotympanum.
Abnormally dark area on a chest x-ray, as from air trapping in foreign body aspiration or emphysema.
A measure of uterine contraction strength, the sum of contraction pressures above baseline in a 10-minute window. Adequate labor is 200 or more.
An oral GnRH antagonist used for pain from endometriosis and fibroids; can cause bone loss.
Compression of the inferior vena cava and aorta by the gravid uterus when a pregnant woman lies supine, reducing venous return and causing hypotension.
A carotid pulse with two systolic peaks, seen in aortic regurgitation and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Small beam-like plates forming the spongy inner network of bone (trabecular bone), or fibrous strands in other organs.
Tilted forward. A normally anteverted uterus tips forward over the bladder.
Between the anterior and middle scalene muscles in the neck, where the brachial plexus passes; interscalene nerve block anesthetizes the shoulder.
A topical vitamin D analog used for plaque psoriasis, slowing keratinocyte growth.
Between seizures. Interictal EEG may show spikes in patients with epilepsy.
Bluish discoloration of the hands and feet, normal in newborns right after birth; scores 1 point on the APGAR appearance criterion.
Inflammation of small vessels, particularly pulmonary capillaries in diffuse alveolar hemorrhage from immune injury, or skin pigmented purpura.
Related to pain caused by activation of pain-sensing nerves (nociceptors) by tissue injury, as opposed to neuropathic pain.
The peritoneal pocket between the bladder and rectum in men. Fluid and urine collect there when the bladder ruptures intraperitoneally.
Placing an endotracheal tube through the nose, used when oral intubation is not possible; contraindicated in midface or skull base fractures.
Emergency surgical airway through an incision in the cricothyroid membrane, used when intubation is not possible.
Rotational eye movement around the visual axis. Upbeat-torsional nystagmus on the Dix-Hallpike maneuver indicates benign paroxysmal positional vertigo.
Contraction of the anal sphincter when the glans or clitoris is squeezed; its return marks the end of spinal shock after spinal cord injury.
Within the bladder; intravesical therapy delivers BCG or chemotherapy directly into the bladder for non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer.
A kinked, elongated aorta that looks like coarctation on imaging but causes no pressure gradient.
Surgical connection of the bile duct to a loop of jejunum, used to drain bile after removal of choledochal cysts or bile duct obstruction.
Large coarse calcium deposits seen on imaging, usually benign in the breast, whereas clustered microcalcifications may signal cancer.
The bony prominences at the ankle: the medial malleolus (tibia) and lateral malleolus (fibula).
Abnormal connection between the aorta and gut (usually duodenum), a rare life-threatening complication after aortic graft repair presenting with GI bleeding.
A radiotracer used in imaging parathyroid adenomas and myocardial perfusion.
Imaging of the urethra with contrast, done to find urethral injury or strictures, e.g., retrograde urethrogram in pelvic fracture.
